specPoints.text: understand how the pressure at a point in a gas or liquid at rest acts equally in all directions
know and use the relationship for pressure difference: pressure difference = height × density × gravitational field strength p = h × ρ × g

primer.text: Divers feel it in their ears: fluid pressure grows with depth. These lessons show why a fluid at rest squeezes equally in all directions, then build the pressure-difference equation that turns depth, density and gravity into pascals.

lessons.title: Pressure in fluids acts in all directions
lessons.opening: A fluid at rest — liquid or gas — pushes on anything immersed in it from every side at once. The squeeze is even, and where it meets a surface the push always arrives head-on, at right angles.
keyPoints: A fluid is a liquid or a gas.
An object at rest in a fluid is squeezed by pressure acting evenly over its whole surface and in all directions.
The fluid's pressure creates forces against the surfaces it touches.
Those forces always act at right angles to the surface.

low.restatement: Sink a ball into water: every point of its skin feels the same steady squeeze, from every compass direction, always straight into the surface. Fluids are democratic squeezers.
low.analogy: A group hug with no favourite side: the water's push arrives from everywhere, each push perpendicular to wherever it lands.
low.examPointer: Draw the force arrows at 90 degrees to the surface in every fluid-pressure diagram — slanted arrows lose the mark.

medium.restatement: For a fluid at rest, pressure at a point is directionless: it acts equally in all directions, delivering normal forces on any immersed surface. The evenness is what distinguishes fluid pressure from a single contact push, and it holds for liquids and gases alike.
medium.analogy: Inflation: a balloon's skin is pressed outward equally everywhere by the air inside — no side is favoured, and every patch is pushed straight out.
medium.examPointer: State 'acts equally in all directions' verbatim for 5.6 — it is the sentence the specification rewards — then attach the right-angle rule for forces.

options.explanation: Both flow, so both are fluids.
Solids are not fluids.
Solids are not fluids.
Gases are fluids too.

check.stem: An object sits stationary in water. How does the water's pressure act on it?

options.text: evenly over its whole surface and in all directions
options.explanation: A fluid at rest squeezes without favourites.
Gravity drives the pressure but not its direction of action.
Every face is squeezed.

options.text: mostly sideways, ignoring top and bottom
options.explanation: The squeeze is even, not lateral.

check.stem: The force a fluid's pressure exerts on an immersed surface acts

options.text: at right angles to that surface
options.explanation: Normal forces only — 90 degrees, always.
Parallel pushes slide nothing here.

options.text: along the object's weight direction only
options.explanation: Weight and fluid force are different pushes.

options.text: in the direction the object is moving
options.explanation: The object is at rest in this scenario.

check.stem: Which everyday observation shows fluid pressure acting in all directions?

options.text: a bubble blown underwater is spherical
options.explanation: Even pressure from all sides rounds the bubble.

options.text: ice floats high in a glass
options.explanation: Floating shows density, not omnidirectionality.
The whistle is steam escaping, not the squeeze.

options.text: a spoon gets hot in soup
options.explanation: That is heating, not pressure.

check.stem: What does the fluid pressure CREATE against an immersed surface?

options.explanation: Pressure delivers forces against surfaces.
Heating is not the pressure's product here.
Nothing optical is involved.
Mass is untouched by pressure.

check.stem: State what the word fluid covers.
check.modelAnswer: A fluid means a liquid or a gas — both flow and both exert pressure.

check.stem: State the direction law for the forces a fluid's pressure exerts on a surface.
check.modelAnswer: The forces act at right angles — 90 degrees — to the surface.

check.stem: Explain why a submerged submarine's hull feels a squeeze from below as well as above.
check.modelAnswer: A fluid at rest carries pressure to every point it touches, acting equally in all directions. The hull's underside faces fluid just as its top does, so the water pushes upward on the keel exactly as it pushes downward and sideways elsewhere — the squeeze has no favoured direction.

check.stem: A toy ball is held still at the bottom of a pool. Describe the water's pushes on the ball's surface.
check.modelAnswer: The water presses evenly over the ball's entire surface and in all directions, with every push arriving at right angles to the skin where it lands.

lessons.title: Pressure difference with depth
sourceHeadings: Pressure in a liquid with a density is applied at a depth
lessons.opening: Dive deeper and the squeeze strengthens: the fluid column above grows heavier. The pressure-difference equation multiplies depth by density by gravitational field strength, and rearranges to predict pressures or depths.
keyPoints: The pressure on an object in a fluid rises as the object sits deeper.
Pressure difference = height × density × gravitational field strength, written p = h × ρ × g.
Height (depth) enters in metres, density in kilograms per metre cubed, g in newtons per kilogram, giving pascals.
The equation rearranges for any of the four quantities — including a depth prediction from a measured pressure.

low.restatement: Every metre down adds another layer of fluid pressing from above, so the deeper you go, the harder the squeeze. Multiply depth by the fluid's density by g and you have the extra pressure in pascals.
low.analogy: A stack of mattresses: the bottom sleeper feels every mattress above; the top sleeper feels none. Depth is position in the stack.
low.examPointer: Rearranging is examined: h = p ÷ (ρ × g) predicts depth from pressure — the swimming-pool style question — and watch the kilopascal conversion.

medium.restatement: The pressure-difference equation p = hρg prices the fluid column above the point of interest: deeper points carry taller columns, denser fluids heavier ones, and g converts mass to weight. It rearranges freely — depth from pressure, density from a measured difference — with all inputs in SI units so the answer lands in pascals.
medium.analogy: A skyscraper's ground-floor lobby carries every floor's weight above it; higher floors feel lighter loads. The lobby is the deep point; the penthouse is the surface.
medium.examPointer: Convert kilopascals to pascals before substituting, and quote pascals or kilopascals consistently in the final line.

check.stem: What happens to the pressure on an object as it sits deeper in a fluid?

options.text: it increases, because the fluid column above it grows
options.explanation: More overlying fluid presses harder.

options.text: it decreases, because the fluid thins with depth
options.explanation: Liquids barely compress; the column grows.

options.text: it stays the same at all depths
options.explanation: Depth is exactly what the equation multiplies.

options.text: it depends only on the object's mass
options.explanation: The object's mass never enters the equation.

check.stem: Which equation gives the pressure difference in a fluid?

options.explanation: Depth times density times field strength.
That is the solid-contact pressure equation.
That is density.
The depth multiplies; it does not divide.

check.stem: Which unit triple feeds p = h × ρ × g so the answer is in pascals?

options.text: metres, kilograms per metre cubed, newtons per kilogram
options.explanation: The SI triple evaluates exactly to pascals.

options.text: centimetres, grams per cm cubed, newtons per kilogram
options.explanation: Mixed units corrupt the pascals.
Density needs its per-volume unit.
None of these fit.

check.stem: A swimmer descends from the surface to 3 m in a pool. The pressure difference she feels depends on

options.text: the water's density, g, and the 3 m depth
options.explanation: Those are exactly the equation's inputs.
Her mass is absent from the equation.
Area never enters this equation.
Temperature is not an input here.

check.stem: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ sits 2 m deep in a tank (g = 10 N/kg). The pressure difference from surface to base is

options.explanation: That slips two factors of ten.
That divides somewhere along the way.
That drops a factor of ten.

check.stem: State the pressure-difference equation in symbols and name each quantity.
check.modelAnswer: p = h × ρ × g, where p is the pressure difference in pascals, h the depth in metres, ρ the fluid's density in kilograms per metre cubed and g the gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram.

check.stem: State how the pressure on an immersed object changes as it moves deeper.
check.modelAnswer: The pressure rises as the object sits deeper, because the fluid column above it grows taller.

check.stem: Explain why the pressure difference depends on the fluid's density.
check.modelAnswer: The overlying column's weight creates the pressure at depth, and weight scales with mass per volume. A denser fluid packs more mass into the same column, so its weight — and the pressure it delivers — is larger for the same depth.

check.stem: A diver measures a pressure difference of 20 kPa in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the depth, and state the rearrangement used.
check.modelAnswer: Rearranged, h = p ÷ (ρ × g) = 20 000 ÷ (1000 × 9.8) ≈ 2.0 m, so the diver sits about two metres deep.

glossary.definition: Either a liquid or a gas — a state that flows and exerts pressure in all directions.
The extra pressure at depth in a fluid, equal to height × density × gravitational field strength.
One thousand pascals, the unit in which large fluid pressures are often quoted.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the depth of water in a swimming pool where a pressure of 20 kPa is exerted. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and the gravitational field strength on Earth is 9.8 N/kg.
steps: List the known quantities: pressure p = 20 kPa, density ρ = 1000 kg/m³, field strength g = 9.8 N/kg.
State the equation: p = h × ρ × g.
Rearrange for depth: h = p ÷ (ρ × g).
workedExample.finalAnswer: The water is about 2.0 m deep where the pressure is 20 kPa.
